profile.summary: LM-Design designs an amino acid sequence for a protein backbone that is given to it (inverse folding). Rather than training a structure model from scratch, it takes an existing protein language model and implants a lightweight structural adapter into it, so the language model's knowledge of natural sequences is reused and given awareness of the fold. At generation time the sequence is refined over several passes. The released checkpoints are built on ESM-1b 650M and ESM-2 650M and trained on CATH 4.2, with one multichain checkpoint for complexes.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; ByProt README.md: Official implementation of LM-Design, Pretrained model weights

summary_quotes.text: We present LM-Design, a generic approach to reprogramming sequence-based protein language models (pLMs), that have learned massive sequential evolutionary knowledge from the universe of natural protein sequences, to acquire an immediate capability to design preferable protein sequences for given folds.

We conduct a structural surgery on pLMs, where a lightweight structural adapter is implanted into pLMs and endows it with structural awareness. During inference, iterative refinement is performed to effectively optimize the generated protein sequences.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A structural adapter is added to a frozen protein language model, which is what the authors call structural surgery. Generation is iterative: the ByProt defaults for LM-Design are five decoding iterations with the denoise strategy, against one iteration and mask_predict for the non-autoregressive ProteinMPNN baseline in the same repository. Sampling temperature defaults to 0, which makes the output deterministic; the README shows how to override it. The HyInv report describes the model's decoding as iterative denoising in five steps.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three LM-Design checkpoints are published in Zenodo deposit 10046338 of 27 October 2023: lm_design_esm1b_650m on CATH 4.2, lm_design_esm2_650m on CATH 4.2, and lm_design_esm2_650m trained on the multichain data for complexes. Each archive is about 1.6 GB. The repository also holds experiment configurations for the ESM-2 series under configs/experiment/fixedbb, but only the 650M checkpoints are released. A result must name the base language model, the training data and the decoding settings, since five iterations at temperature 0 is not the same run as five iterations at temperature 0.1.
sections.source_locator: ByProt README.md: Pretrained model weights, Example 2; Zenodo files and publication_date

sections.title: What is reported about it
sections.body: The paper's abstract claims gains of 4 to 12 per cent in sequence recovery over the state of the art at the time, giving 55.65 per cent on CATH 4.2 and 56.63 per cent on CATH 4.3 for single chains and above 60 per cent for complexes. The repository's own worked example recovers 0.76 of the native sequence on one backbone, against 0.37 for the CMLM baseline. Separately, the HyInv report used LM-Design 650M as one of ten published baselines and puts its own model ahead by 0.044 scTM on average, while noting that LM-Design is among the parallel decoders that sample at lower diversity. All of these are their authors' figures, not Rewire's.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; ByProt README.md: Example 2 output; HyInv report Section 5.2 and Table 7

quotes.text: leading to up to 4% to 12% accuracy gains in sequence recovery (e.g., 55.65%/56.63% on CATH 4.2/4.3 single-chain benchmarks, and >60% when designing protein complexes)

Parallel decoders (PiFold, CMLM,
LM-Design, DPLM-2) sample at much lower diversity and have the lowest scTM.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: CATH 4.2 for the two single-chain checkpoints, in the preprocessed form from Ingraham et al. 2019; the multichain checkpoint uses the PDB complex data curated for ProteinMPNN. The repository also supports CATH 4.3 from Hsu et al. 2022.

This dataset curated protein (multichain) complexies from Protein Data Bank (PDB).

run_guide.summary: Install ByProt, download the ESM-2 650M LM-Design checkpoint and design a sequence for one PDB backbone.
prerequisites: Conda with Python 3.7, as the repository's installation block sets up.
A GPU: the designer example sets cuda=True.
About 1.6 GB for the checkpoint archive, plus a backbone PDB file.
Code is Apache-2.0; the checkpoints on Zenodo are CC BY 4.0.

steps.title: Design a sequence for one backbone
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from byprot.utils.config import compose_config as Cfg
from byprot.tasks.fixedbb.designer import Designer

# 1. instantialize designer
exp_path = "run/logs/fixedbb/cath_4.2/lm_design_esm2_650m"
cfg = Cfg(
    cuda=True,
    generator=Cfg(
        max_iter=5,
        strategy='denoise', 
        temperature=0,
        eval_sc=False,  
    )
)
designer = Designer(experiment_path=exp_path, cfg=cfg)

# 2. load structure from pdb file
pdb_path = "data/3uat_variants/3uat_GK.pdb"
designer.set_structure(pdb_path)

# 3. generate sequence from the given structure
designer.generate()

# 4. calculate evaluation metircs
designer.calculate_metrics()
PY
steps.explanation: Copied from the README's Example 2, wrapped by Rewire in a shell heredoc, with the two absolute placeholder paths replaced by paths relative to the clone and the optional second generate call left out.

notes: Points for a reviewer. The 650M parameter figure is the base language model named in the checkpoint name and in the HyInv report's label LM-Design 650M; the structural adapter's own size is not published, so the structured rows do not separate the two. The paper was read only as its arXiv abstract. This record shares all of its sources with the CMLM record, because ByProt releases both and presents CMLM as its non-autoregressive ProteinMPNN baseline; a reviewer may want to link the two records. The HyInv report's comparison is that project's own evaluation, and it groups LM-Design with the parallel decoders even though the repository's default strategy for it is iterative denoising over five steps. Quotes from the HyInv report come from a pdftotext text layer, so line breaks inside them follow the PDF layout.
